en: *Hastavālaprakaraṇa*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by imperial decree.
The treatise states:
It is held that within the three realms there exist only provisional designations and no external objects in reality, due to the force of false attachment.

Now, desiring to provide a definitive analysis of the gateway to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena for those who have not yet realized the truth, so that they may attain an unerring understanding, this treatise is composed.
The verse says:
Just as one perceives a snake where there is only a rope, Upon seeing the rope, one knows the object is non-existent;
If one analyzes its constituent parts, One knows that the perception of a snake was an error.
The treatise says:

Just as when one sees something resembling a rope or a snake at a place that is neither far nor clearly defined, and being unable to discern their distinct intrinsic natures due to delusion, one resolutely grasps it as a snake.
Later, having understood those differentiated phenomena, one knows that they arise from the delusion of false attachment; thus, they are merely misconceptions and lack any substantial reality.
Furthermore, when one carefully examines the distinct parts of the rope itself, even the self-nature of the rope cannot be found.
Having understood this, all the knots of the rope are untied, like the realization that it was a snake; there is only deluded consciousness.

Just as there was a delusive consciousness regarding the rope, so too regarding its parts, such as the strands and so forth, one knows that their characteristics are mutually dependent and no real substance can be found. Therefore, the mental images associated with the mind that take the rope and its parts as objects are merely deluded consciousness.
The verse says:
When all things that are conventionally designated are minutely examined in terms of their intrinsic nature,
they are found to be merely nominal in relation to others, even down to the objects of worldly convention.
The treatise says:

Just as when one analytically examines and scrutinizes the constituent parts of a rope and so forth individually, one knows that there is no substantial entity, and that it is merely a product of the deluded mind.

Thus it should be understood that all phenomena are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). For example, objects such as jars and garments are formed by depending on clay, threads, and so forth; as long as they remain within the sphere of verbal expression and cognitive activity until their destruction, they are designated as "jars" and the like.
Regarding the phrase "derived from others," this means that [the self] exists by way of conventional discourse, not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
The verse states:
Because it is partless and not perceived, And because it is equally non-existent at the limit of analysis.
"Only due to a deluded mind; the wise should not cling to it.
The treatise says:

If one further clings to the view that all provisional phenomena remain indivisible even when reduced to the state of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and that these atoms, being devoid of spatial parts, are substantially existent—this is just like a flower in the sky or the horns of a rabbit. Because they cannot be seen and lack the power to produce the consciousness that takes them as its object, the atoms thus clung to are certainly not substantially existent.
Therefore, it must be stated that the cause is imperceptible, because one cannot establish that atoms exist as substantial realities.
Why is this so? Because they possess spatial dimensions and distinctions of location.

Just as when one perceives existing objects such as jars or garments, or directions such as east, west, north, and south, these are all currently perceived as having constituent parts that can be identified because they are differentiated by direction.
If it is claimed that atoms are currently existent, they must necessarily possess directional parts, because they possess the nature of distinct differentiation.
In that case, one must admit the differentiation of directions such as east, west, north, and so forth.
Thus, the theory of these being real atoms is not established;
nor are they a single entity, because they possess multiple parts and because their perceived appearances differ.
A single, ultimate atom cannot be definitively apprehended; thus, one should abandon the theory of atoms.
Therefore, the wise understand that the three realms are entirely products of deluded perception; in seeking the sublime principle, one should not cling to reality.
The verse says:
Because that which falsely exists is not real, it differs from what is seen;
since the characteristics of the object are illusory, the perceiving subject as well does not exist.
The treatise says:

If one claims that regarding objects such as those jars and garments, we also admit that their intrinsic nature is unapprehendable and that they are all merely discriminated by deluded consciousness, yet the confused consciousness that takes those appearances as its object is substantially real—just as when observing a city of gandharvas or illusory persons, the consciousness thereof exists.
Even if this consciousness exists, it is not real because it does not correspond to the perceived object.
This deluded consciousness forms an understanding of existence with respect to its objective referent.

Since the intrinsic nature of those objects has already been clarified as non-existent, and since the objects are thus absent, the deluded consciousness that takes them as its objective support is likewise not truly existent; how, then, could one cause that deluded consciousness to exist?
However, have you never seen in the world that there is no seed capable of producing a sprout that is produced?
For this reason, the logic of your analogies, such as the illusory city, is not established.
The verse says:
All these are mere designations; the well-awakened one is able to know them.
When the wise person cuts off the afflictions, it is as easy as removing the fear of a snake.
The treatise says:

As it is said, the three realms exist only as provisional designations; once coarse perceptions of things such as jars have been eliminated, one knows that their existence arises from names and conventions.
Once those with skillful observation have understood this, the fear of a snake at the place where there is only a rope is dispelled;
furthermore, through careful reflection, they discern its distinctions, and even the false attachment to the rope and so forth ceases to exist.

When observing in this manner, all dharmas capable of producing detachment from defilement will easily and swiftly eliminate the net of afflictions, and the various karmic fruits shall naturally be severed and extinguished.
There is another verse that says:
When a wise person observes worldly affairs, They should act in accordance with worldly conventions;
Yet, if they wish to seek the severance of afflictions, They must clarify the true ultimate truth.
Just as worldly people regard common things such as jars and garments as being substantially existent,
calling them "jars" and "garments," so too should the wise person employ conventional speech in accordance with the world, while knowing that these things do not exist substantially.

If one delights in observing the faults of afflictions and seeks liberation, one should thoroughly investigate and apply correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) within this true ultimate reality; thus, the bonds of affliction—the deluded consciousnesses that take objects as their referents—will no longer arise.
*Hastavālaprakaraṇa*, one fascicle.
